title: Understanding IRD: Taxes on a Decedent's Unpaid Income (November 2026)
summary: This November 2026 guide explains income in respect of a decedent, common IRD items, and how estates report them.
body_markdown:
After a death, income the person earned or was owed but had not yet received, known as income in respect of a decedent (IRD), is taxed to the estate or the beneficiary who receives the money. Which return reports the income depends on who receives the money and when. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: what counts as IRD, common examples such as final paychecks and inherited IRAs, who has authority to act and who reports the income, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- IRD is income earned before death but received after, taxed to the estate or recipient.
- Traditional IRA, 401(k), annuity, and final paycheck payouts are common IRD items.
- The estate reports IRD on Form 1041, and beneficiaries report their share on Form 1040.
- Beneficiaries may deduct federal estate tax tied to IRD under section 691(c).
- Elayne requests 10 years of IRS tax transcripts to point to accounts and unpaid income.


## What Is Income in Respect of a Decedent?


Income in respect of a decedent (IRD) is income a person earned or had a right to receive before death but had not yet received, or properly included, on their final income tax return. That final return generally covers only income received through the date of death, so money that arrives afterward falls outside it.


IRD is taxed to whoever receives it, whether the estate or a beneficiary. This rule comes from section 691 of the Internal Revenue Code, and[Publication 559](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p559) describes how the rule applies to families and executors.

## Common Examples of Income in Respect of a Decedent


Item Why It Is IRD Who Typically Reports It


Final paycheck, accrued vacation pay, unpaid commissions Earned before death, paid after Estate or recipient


[Traditional IRA, 401(k), pension balances](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-a-401-k-works-after-death) Never taxed Named beneficiary


Annuity payments Untaxed gains paid out Beneficiary


Savings bond interest, installment sale payments, unpaid rent or royalties Earned but not yet received Estate or recipient


Items generally not IRD include life insurance death benefits and property with a stepped-up basis.


## What Is an IRD Check?


An IRD check is a payment issued after a death for pay or[retirement benefits](https://www.elayne.com/resources/discovering-401-k-and-retirement-benefits-after-a-death) the person had earned, such as a final paycheck, a commission, or a deferred compensation payout. "IRD" describes why the money exists: it was owed to the person who died.


The payer typically reports the amount on Form W-2 or Form 1099 under the recipient's name and tax ID, meaning the estate or the beneficiary. When a figure appears under the decedent's name, Publication 559 includes a worksheet for matching it to the correct return.


## Who Has Authority and Who Reports IRD?


The personal representative acts for the estate: the executor named in a will, an administrator appointed when there is no will, or a person using a simplified small-estate process. Authority comes from court documents (letters testamentary or letters of administration), and Form 56 notifies the IRS of the fiduciary. The estate needs its own EIN for Form 1041.


Under[section 691(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/691) , the person entitled to the income is taxed on it.


When the estate receives the right to the income, the estate reports it on Form 1041. When the right passes directly to a beneficiary by designation or survivorship, the beneficiary reports it on their own return.


IRD is taxed in the year it is received, which is often after the year of death.


## Why IRD Can Be Hard to Spot: Finding What the Person Was Owed


IRD is easy to miss because no single list of it exists. Unpaid wages, retirement accounts, annuities, and deferred compensation sit with different payers.


Payer filings help point to sources. A Form 1099-R suggests a retirement plan or annuity, and a Form W-2 points to an employer who may owe final pay. Free public resources also help locate accounts:


- State unclaimed property databases
- MissingMoney.com
- The NAIC life insurance policy locator
- The PBGC pension search


These resources are part of the broader process of[finding a deceased person's assets](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-assets-deceased-person) .

## How Elayne Helps Families Account for Income Owed After a Death


Income in respect of a decedent often sits with payers the family does not know about, because no single record lists what a person was owed. A will names who inherits, but a will is not an inventory of accounts or of income still owed. Elayne is an online service that helps families settle an estate, and Elayne's Asset Search builds an inventory of what the person owned and owed.


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) holds IRS authorization to request 10 years of the person's IRS tax transcripts. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return: a transcript lists what banks, brokerages, employers, insurers, and retirement custodians reported about the person to the IRS. Each reporting institution points to a possible account, employer, or plan. An employer that reported wages may still owe final pay, and a retirement custodian that reported a distribution may hold an account with untaxed funds, both of which are common sources of IRD.


Elayne also requests the person's Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, cards, and debts in the person's name, and checks 100+ other sources. These sources include the life insurance locators, the pension registry, the national unclaimed property database, and property and vehicle records.


Every finding is listed with the source that reported the finding, and debts appear alongside assets, so the estate's obligations are visible before any money is paid out. The inventory is organized in this order: retirement accounts, bank and brokerage accounts, life insurance, property, business interests, and debts. If the search finds nothing new, the family still receives a documented record that the search was done, along with whether the estate owes the IRS anything and which debts are open.


Legal authority controls who can act. Banks, insurers, and retirement custodians generally release information and money only to a person the court has authorized to act for the estate. The court issues that authority as letters testamentary when a will names an executor, or as letters of administration when an administrator is appointed. Portions of the Asset Search can run before the court paper is issued, and the full search opens once legal authority is in place.


Asset Search includes a 1:1 call with an Estate Expert to walk through the findings, with slots open within 24 hours. The personal representative, meaning the executor or administrator, holds the authority to act for the estate. Reporting decisions, such as which return an item of IRD belongs on, are made by the personal representative together with an attorney or CPA the estate works with, and those professionals can work from the same estate record, including the inventory and account history.

## FAQ


### What happens to an inherited IRA if I miss the required minimum distribution deadline?


A missed required minimum distribution from an inherited IRA triggers a 25 percent excise tax on the amount that should have been withdrawn, reported on Form 5329. The IRS may reduce or waive the penalty when the shortfall resulted from a reasonable error and the missed amount has been withdrawn.


### Can I find out what income a loved one was still owed without a list of accounts?


Yes. A will is not an inventory, but 10 years of IRS tax transcripts can show which employers, banks, insurers, and retirement custodians reported payments to the person, and a W-2 or Form 1099-R can point to final pay or an IRA that still holds untaxed funds. Elayne holds IRS authorization to request those transcripts and checks 100+ other sources, building a source-attributed inventory with debts listed beside assets. Free searches such as MissingMoney.com, the NAIC life insurance locator, and the PBGC pension search add to the picture.


### Is an IRD check taxed to the estate or to the beneficiary who deposits it?


It is taxed to whoever is entitled to receive the money, and the payer's Form W-2 or 1099 normally lists the estate or the beneficiary. When the check is paid to the estate, the estate reports it on Form 1041, and a beneficiary who receives the funds directly reports them on their own return in the year of receipt.


### How do I help protect the identity of a person who died?


The credit bureaus can be notified of the death with a deceased notification so no new credit can be opened in the person's name, and the mail can be forwarded so tax forms and legal notices are not missed. Elayne sends the deceased notification to the credit bureaus in Estate Setup, and Estate Settlement adds ongoing Equifax identity protection monitoring of the person's credit file. Keeping copies of the death certificate on hand helps make each of these notifications faster.
